questions.title: Spring Boot Actuator
questions.question: What is Spring Boot Actuator and why is it useful?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Production-ready features:** health, metrics, info, env — out of the box
- **HTTP endpoints:** expose operational data over HTTP (or JMX)
- **Security by default:** most endpoints are secured/disabled by default in Boot 2+
- **Micrometer integration:** metrics are backed by Micrometer, not raw counters
- **Red flag:** only knowing `/health` — show awareness of the full endpoint catalogue

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Spring Boot Actuator adds production-ready operational endpoints to your application with zero configuration. Once you add the `spring-boot-starter-actuator` dependency, you immediately get HTTP endpoints for health checks, metrics, environment inspection, thread dumps, heap dumps, and much more.

In a production environment, Actuator is what your monitoring system talks to. Kubernetes uses `/actuator/health` for liveness and readiness probes. Prometheus scrapes `/actuator/prometheus` for metrics. Your ops team uses `/actuator/env` to verify configuration without SSH-ing into servers.

Security-wise, only `/actuator/health` and `/actuator/info` are exposed over HTTP by default. You explicitly enable others via `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include`. This default-closed approach is intentional — endpoints like `/actuator/env` and `/actuator/heapdump` expose sensitive data and must be deliberately opened and secured.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Key Endpoints

| Endpoint | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `/actuator/health` | App and dependency health status |
| `/actuator/metrics` | Counter, gauge, timer metrics |
| `/actuator/info` | App version, git info, custom data |
| `/actuator/env` | All environment properties |
| `/actuator/loggers` | View/change log levels at runtime |
| `/actuator/mappings` | All registered request mappings |
| `/actuator/threaddump` | JVM thread dump |
| `/actuator/prometheus` | Prometheus-format metrics |

## Enabling Endpoints

```properties
# Expose all endpoints over HTTP
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=*

# Expose specific endpoints
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,metrics,loggers

# Change base path (default is /actuator)
management.endpoints.web.base-path=/management

# Run actuator on a different port (recommended for internal-only access)
management.server.port=8081
```

## Production Reality

Run Actuator on a separate management port (`management.server.port=8081`) and restrict that port to your internal network via firewall rules. This is simpler and more reliable than trying to secure individual endpoints with Spring Security rules.

questions.title: Health Endpoint
questions.question: What information does the /actuator/health endpoint provide?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Aggregated status:** UP, DOWN, OUT_OF_SERVICE, UNKNOWN
- **Component-level health:** DB, disk, cache, messaging — each has its own indicator
- **Liveness vs Readiness:** Boot 2.3+ added separate probes for Kubernetes
- **`show-details`:** controls whether component details are visible to all or just authenticated users
- **Red flag:** thinking health only checks if the JVM is running

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The `/actuator/health` endpoint provides an aggregated health status for your application — either `UP`, `DOWN`, `OUT_OF_SERVICE`, or `UNKNOWN`. It combines health indicators from all registered components: the database connection, disk space, Redis, RabbitMQ, and any custom indicators you write.

In Spring Boot 2.3 and later, the endpoint also exposes separate liveness and readiness probes under `/actuator/health/liveness` and `/actuator/health/readiness`. This is specifically designed for Kubernetes: liveness tells Kubernetes whether to restart the pod, readiness tells it whether to send traffic.

By default, the endpoint shows only the top-level status. You control detail visibility with `management.endpoint.health.show-details`, which can be `never`, `always`, or `when-authorized`. In production, `when-authorized` is the right choice — component details like database connection info are sensitive.

questions.title: Custom HealthIndicator
questions.question: How do you implement a custom HealthIndicator?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **`HealthIndicator` interface:** implement `health()` method, return `Health` object
- **`@Component`:** register it as a Spring bean and Actuator picks it up automatically
- **`Health.up()` / `Health.down()`:** builder methods with optional detail map
- **Naming convention:** bean name `fooHealthIndicator` → shows as `foo` in `/health` response
- **Red flag:** throwing exceptions instead of returning `Health.down()` — exceptions crash the endpoint

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Implementing a custom `HealthIndicator` is straightforward. You create a class that implements the `HealthIndicator` interface, annotate it with `@Component`, and implement the `health()` method to return a `Health` object.

The `Health` class has builder methods: `Health.up()` for healthy, `Health.down()` for unhealthy, and `Health.unknown()` for indeterminate state. You can chain `.withDetail(key, value)` to add context that appears in the health response when details are enabled.

Spring Boot discovers your indicator automatically by component scan and names it in the health response using the bean name — strip the `HealthIndicator` suffix and you get the component key. So a bean named `paymentGatewayHealthIndicator` appears as `paymentGateway` in the JSON response.

speakable_v2.hook: Implementing a custom HealthIndicator is straightforward.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

questions.title: Micrometer Integration
questions.question: How does Actuator integrate with Micrometer for metrics collection?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Micrometer is the facade:** like SLF4J for logging, Micrometer abstracts metrics backends
- **`MeterRegistry`:** the central interface — inject it to record metrics
- **Auto-configured JVM metrics:** GC, heap, thread counts come free with Actuator
- **Backend-agnostic:** switch from Prometheus to Datadog by changing a dependency
- **Red flag:** confusing Micrometer with Prometheus — Prometheus is one possible backend

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Spring Boot Actuator uses Micrometer as its metrics instrumentation library. Micrometer is to metrics what SLF4J is to logging — a vendor-neutral facade that lets you write instrumentation code once and publish to any monitoring backend by swapping a dependency.

When you add `spring-boot-starter-actuator`, Spring Boot auto-configures a `MeterRegistry` based on what's on the classpath. Add `micrometer-registry-prometheus` and you get a Prometheus-compatible registry. Add `micrometer-registry-datadog` instead and metrics flow to Datadog. Your instrumentation code never changes.

Out of the box, Micrometer automatically instruments JVM metrics — heap usage, GC pause times, thread counts, class loading — and HTTP server metrics — request counts, latencies, response codes — all without any code you write. You inject `MeterRegistry` to add your own business metrics on top.

questions.title: Custom Metrics with Micrometer
questions.question: How do you create and publish custom metrics using Micrometer?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Three main types:** `Counter` (count events), `Gauge` (current value), `Timer` (duration + count)
- **Inject `MeterRegistry`:** the entry point for registering all meter types
- **Tags:** key-value dimensions that let you slice metrics in the monitoring system
- **`@Timed` annotation:** AOP-based timer for methods — less code than manual Timer
- **Red flag:** creating a new meter on every request — meters should be created once and reused

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Micrometer provides three main metric types. A `Counter` monotonically increases — use it to count events like orders created or errors thrown. A `Gauge` tracks a current value that can go up or down — use it for queue depth, active sessions, or cache size. A `Timer` measures the duration of operations and also counts their invocations.

You inject `MeterRegistry` into your service and create meters using its fluent API. The important thing is to create meters once — typically in the constructor or with `@PostConstruct` — and reuse them. Creating a meter on every method call is wasteful and produces duplicate registrations.

Tags are how you make metrics queryable. Instead of creating a separate counter for each order type, you create one counter with a `type` tag. In Prometheus or Grafana, you then filter or group by that tag.

questions.title: Prometheus Metrics Exposure
questions.question: How do you expose metrics in Prometheus format?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Add `micrometer-registry-prometheus` dependency:** that's all it takes
- **`/actuator/prometheus` endpoint:** auto-configured, scraped by Prometheus server
- **Prometheus scrape config:** show you know how Prometheus pulls data (pull model)
- **Naming convention:** Micrometer converts dots to underscores for Prometheus format
- **Red flag:** thinking you configure Prometheus inside Spring Boot — Prometheus pulls, Spring Boot exposes

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Exposing Prometheus-format metrics requires adding one dependency — `micrometer-registry-prometheus`. Spring Boot auto-configures a `PrometheusMeterRegistry` and exposes the `/actuator/prometheus` endpoint, which Prometheus scrapes on its polling interval.

Prometheus uses a pull model: your application doesn't push metrics to Prometheus. Instead, your Prometheus server is configured with a scrape job that hits `/actuator/prometheus` every 15 or 30 seconds and stores the snapshot. This is why you don't need any Prometheus-specific code in your application — just expose the endpoint.

One naming detail to know: Micrometer converts metric names from dot-separated to underscore-separated for Prometheus compatibility. So `http.server.requests` becomes `http_server_requests_seconds_count` in the Prometheus output.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Setup

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId>
    <artifactId>micrometer-registry-prometheus</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

```properties
# Expose the prometheus endpoint
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=prometheus,health,info
```

## Prometheus Scrape Configuration

```yaml
# prometheus.yml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: 'spring-boot-app'
    metrics_path: '/actuator/prometheus'
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['app-host:8080']
    scrape_interval: 15s
```

## Sample Output Format

```
# HELP http_server_requests_seconds Duration of HTTP server request handling
# TYPE http_server_requests_seconds summary
http_server_requests_seconds_count{method="GET",status="200",uri="/api/users"} 1547
http_server_requests_seconds_sum{method="GET",status="200",uri="/api/users"} 12.438
```

## With Grafana Dashboard

Combine with Grafana for visualisation. The Spring Boot Micrometer Grafana dashboard (ID 4701) works out of the box with these metrics.

## Production Reality

When running multiple instances, Prometheus scrapes each pod separately and aggregates with `sum()` or `rate()` in PromQL. Make sure your metrics don't include instance-specific IDs in metric names — use labels/tags for instance identification instead.

questions.title: Dynamic Log Level Changes
questions.question: How do you dynamically change logging levels using /actuator/loggers?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **No restart needed:** change log levels at runtime via HTTP POST
- **GET to inspect, POST to change:** know both operations
- **Package-level granularity:** can change level for a specific package or class
- **Temporary — not persisted:** levels reset on app restart
- **Depth signal:** mention this is invaluable for production debugging without redeployment

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The `/actuator/loggers` endpoint lets you change log levels at runtime without restarting the application. This is one of the most practically useful Actuator features in production — when you're debugging an issue and need more verbose logging, you POST to the endpoint to temporarily enable DEBUG or TRACE level for a specific package, investigate, and then revert.

To inspect the current level: `GET /actuator/loggers/com.example.service`. To change it: POST to the same URL with a JSON body `{"configuredLevel": "DEBUG"}`. To reset to the configured default: POST with `{"configuredLevel": null}`.

The change is not persisted — it lives only in the running JVM. If the pod restarts, levels revert to what's in your configuration files. That's usually fine for debugging sessions, but if you want persistent changes, update your configuration source.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Enabling the Endpoint

```properties
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=loggers
```

## GET — Inspect Levels

```bash
# Get all loggers
curl http://localhost:8080/actuator/loggers

# Get specific logger
curl http://localhost:8080/actuator/loggers/com.example.service
```

Response:
```json
{
  "configuredLevel": null,
  "effectiveLevel": "INFO"
}
```
`configuredLevel` is what you explicitly set; `effectiveLevel` is what's actually used (inherits from parent if null).

## POST — Change Level

```bash
# Enable DEBUG for a package
curl -X POST \
  http://localhost:8080/actuator/loggers/com.example.service \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"configuredLevel": "DEBUG"}'

# Reset to default
curl -X POST \
  http://localhost:8080/actuator/loggers/com.example.service \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"configuredLevel": null}'
```

## Production Reality

Pair this with a runbook: when on-call, before enabling DEBUG logging in production, first check if the issue reproduces with INFO. DEBUG logs can be extremely verbose (every SQL query, every HTTP request header) and can fill disk quickly or overwhelm your log aggregation system.

questions.title: Actuator Endpoints Overview
questions.question: What are the main Actuator endpoints and what do they provide?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Know at least 6-8 endpoints by name and purpose:** health, metrics, info, env, loggers, mappings, beans, heapdump
- **Security defaults:** only health and info exposed over HTTP by default
- **Separate management port:** best practice to isolate actuator from app traffic
- **`/actuator` root:** lists all available endpoint links
- **Red flag:** only knowing `/health` and `/metrics`

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Spring Boot Actuator ships with a rich catalogue of endpoints. The most commonly used ones are: `/health` for application and dependency health, `/metrics` to query individual metrics by name, `/info` for application metadata like version and git commit, `/env` to inspect all environment properties and their sources, `/loggers` for runtime log level management, `/mappings` to list all registered HTTP endpoints, `/beans` to inspect the Spring bean graph, and `/threaddump` and `/heapdump` for JVM diagnostic data.

By default, only `/health` and `/info` are exposed over HTTP — everything else requires explicit opt-in via `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include`. The recommended production setup is to run Actuator on a separate port with `management.server.port` set to an internal-only port, and then you can safely expose all endpoints on that port without worrying about public access.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Full Endpoint Reference

| Endpoint | HTTP | Default Exposed | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/health` | GET | Yes | Health status |
| `/info` | GET | Yes | App metadata |
| `/metrics/{name}` | GET | No | Specific metric |
| `/env` | GET | No | All properties |
| `/loggers` | GET/POST | No | Log levels |
| `/mappings` | GET | No | Request mappings |
| `/beans` | GET | No | Spring beans |
| `/threaddump` | GET | No | Thread stack traces |
| `/heapdump` | GET | No | Heap dump file |
| `/scheduledtasks` | GET | No | Scheduled tasks |
| `/caches` | GET/DELETE | No | Cache management |
| `/prometheus` | GET | No | Prometheus metrics |

## Configuration

```properties
# Expose all (only safe behind firewall/VPN)
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=*

# Specific endpoints for production
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,prometheus,loggers

# Separate secure port for internal access
management.server.port=8081
management.server.address=127.0.0.1
```

## Production Reality

`/actuator/beans` lists every Spring bean with its class and dependencies — useful for debugging but exposes your internal architecture. `/actuator/env` shows all properties including potentially sensitive ones (though values with "password" in the key are masked). These should never be on a public-facing port.

speakable_v2.hook: Spring Boot Actuator ships with a rich catalogue of endpoints.
speakable_v2.cap: The recommended production setup is to run Actuator on a separate port with management.server.port set to an internal-only port, and then you can safely expose all endpoints on that port without worry

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **`/actuator/metrics`:** lists all metric names
- **`/actuator/metrics/{name}`:** queries a specific metric with optional tag filters
- **Auto-configured groups:** JVM, HTTP, process, Hikari, cache metrics come free
- **Tag-based filtering:** `/actuator/metrics/http.server.requests?tag=status:200`
- **Red flag:** not knowing you can filter by tags from the URL

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The `/actuator/metrics` endpoint lists all metric names registered in the `MeterRegistry`. You then query individual metrics by navigating to `/actuator/metrics/{metricName}`. The response shows the current value along with all available tags for that metric.

Out of the box, Spring Boot auto-configures a comprehensive set of metrics. JVM metrics cover heap and non-heap memory, GC pause times and counts, thread states, and class loading. HTTP metrics track request counts, latencies, and status codes for every mapped endpoint. If you use HikariCP, connection pool stats like active connections, pending threads, and connection timeouts are also automatically tracked.

Tag filtering is the powerful feature — you can narrow a metric down. For example, `/actuator/metrics/http.server.requests?tag=status:500` shows only your 500-error rate, or add `tag=uri:/api/users` to isolate one endpoint's metrics.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Querying Metrics

```bash
# List all metric names
GET /actuator/metrics

# Query a metric
GET /actuator/metrics/http.server.requests
```

Response:
```json
{
  "name": "http.server.requests",
  "measurements": [
    { "statistic": "COUNT", "value": 15240 },
    { "statistic": "TOTAL_TIME", "value": 127.5 },
    { "statistic": "MAX", "value": 2.3 }
  ],
  "availableTags": [
    { "tag": "method", "values": ["GET", "POST", "PUT"] },
    { "tag": "status", "values": ["200", "404", "500"] },
    { "tag": "uri", "values": ["/api/users", "/api/orders"] }
  ]
}
```

## Tag Filtering

```bash
# Only 500 errors
GET /actuator/metrics/http.server.requests?tag=status:500

# Errors on a specific endpoint
GET /actuator/metrics/http.server.requests?tag=status:500&tag=uri:/api/orders
```

## Auto-Configured Metric Categories

- **JVM:** `jvm.memory.*`, `jvm.gc.*`, `jvm.threads.*`
- **HTTP:** `http.server.requests`
- **Process:** `process.cpu.usage`, `process.uptime`
- **Hikari:** `hikaricp.connections.*`
- **Logback:** `logback.events` (count by level)
- **Tomcat:** `tomcat.sessions.*`

## Production Reality

The `/actuator/metrics` HTTP interface is fine for ad-hoc checks but not for dashboards. For operational monitoring, scrape with Prometheus and visualise in Grafana — they handle time-series aggregation and alerting properly.

speakable_v2.cap: For example, /actuator/metrics/http.server.requests?tag=status:500 shows only your 500-error rate, or add tag=uri:/api/users to isolate one endpoint's metrics.

questions.title: Request Mappings Endpoint
questions.question: How do you view all request mappings using /actuator/mappings?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Lists all registered HTTP endpoints:** including auto-configured ones (Actuator, error, static resources)
- **Request details per mapping:** method, path, produces/consumes content types, handler class
- **Useful for debugging:** verify an endpoint is registered or find conflicting mappings
- **Includes non-controller mappings:** resource handlers, Actuator endpoints themselves
- **Red flag:** not knowing it exists — it's a commonly forgotten but useful endpoint

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The `/actuator/mappings` endpoint lists every HTTP endpoint registered in your application — your controllers, Actuator's own endpoints, error handlers, and static resource mappings. Each entry shows the HTTP method, URL pattern, the handler class and method, and what media types it produces or consumes.

In practice it's most useful in two situations. First, when you're not sure if a new endpoint is being picked up — maybe the controller is in the wrong package or has a typo in the path. Second, when debugging routing conflicts or trying to understand which handler handles a given request pattern. Rather than reading through controller code, you get a flat list of all mappings in one place.

Enable it with `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=mappings` and hit GET on `/actuator/mappings`.
